abstract: Mutations in the dynein heavy chain gene (DYNC1H1) cause a spectrum of neurological disorders, including malformations of cortical development (MCD) and spinal muscular atrophy with lower extremity predominance (SMALED). How these mutations differentially affect dynein functions in the nervous system, leading to distinct pathologies, remains unknown. Using patient-derived cortical organoids, we address how MCD- and SMALED-causing dynein mutations alter human cortical development. We show that MCD-associated mutations alter the growth of organoids, but that SMALED organoids are unaffected, consistent with the microcephaly phenotypes of individuals with MCD. These defects are mirrored by a large increase in apoptotic cell death in MCD organoids. MCD mutations - but not SMALED mutations - strongly affect radial glial progenitor divisions, by inducing severe mitotic spindle defects and leading to prolonged mitotic duration. Mitotic checkpoint inhibition alleviates mitotic delay but fails to prevent apoptosis, indicating that mitotic arrest is not the cause of cell death in MCD. These findings reveal how specific dynein mutations can distinctly disrupt cortical development, establishing mitotic spindle dysfunction and apoptosis as central mechanisms underlying dynein-related microcephaly.
